title: Halsey's carriers hit Manila again
pull: Three hundred fifty planes over the bay

facts.text: On 13 November 1944, carrier planes of Admiral William Halsey's Task Force 38 struck Japanese shipping in and around Manila Bay in the Philippines.
More than 350 carrier planes went after the light cruiser Kiso as she got under way in the bay. Their carriers included Hornet, Essex, Ticonderoga, Enterprise, and four light carriers.
Kiso had orders to leave for Brunei that evening, carrying Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima and his staff.
Between about 8:00 and 9:23 a.m. three bombs hit her, in the bow, near the boiler rooms, and near the aft guns. She lost power and settled into the shallow water west of Cavite that afternoon.
Accounts of her losses differ: Pacific Wrecks gives 89 killed and 105 wounded, while another count says 175 men went down with her and 104 survived.
At Cavite, the destroyers Akishimo and Akebono were moored side by side when bombs set both ablaze. A huge explosion aboard Akishimo the next day wrecked them both.
Other Japanese destroyers and transports were also sunk in and around the bay that day, among them the destroyer Okinami.
A U.S. Navy cameraman flying with the strike filmed Avenger torpedo bombers in close formation, ships maneuvering in the bay, and columns of smoke rising over the Manila waterfront.
Japan salvaged Kiso's wreck in 1955 and broke her up for scrap in 1956.

sources.title: Strike on Manila Bay Area (428-NPC-6221), U.S. National Archives

photoNote: The wrecked Japanese destroyer Okinami, sunk by U.S. carrier planes on 13 November 1944, lying in the shallows of Manila Bay with the city behind, photographed in February 1945. U.S. Navy photo via the Naval History and Heritage Command, public domain (via Wikimedia Commons, 1880 px original). Three months after the strike; the caption should say so. No public domain photo of the 13 November attack itself was found online (80-G-272703 is listed as a Ticonderoga strike photo of 13 Nov but is not digitized at NARA).
photoCredit: The wreck of the Japanese destroyer Okinami, sunk on 13 November 1944, in Manila Bay, February 1945. U.S. Navy photo, Naval History and Heritage Command, public domain.

declassified.fact: Kiso's wreck sat in Manila Bay for more than ten years. A Japanese salvage company raised her on 15 December 1955, and she was cut up for scrap in the bay the next month.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Navy film 'Strike on Manila Bay Area', dated 13 Nov 1944 in the NARA catalog (no slate seen). Silent. A burned in timecode runs along the bottom 12 percent of the frame, so crop it out. The file is the stretch from 0:14 to 9:11 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times: 0:00 to 1:00 aerial views over Manila; 1:58 to 2:35 an Avenger flies in close formation beside the camera plane, the best moving opener; 3:35 to 4:25 ships maneuvering in the bay, with a wake at about 4:18; 4:30 to 4:55 heavy smoke over the harbor; 5:35 to 7:20 burning ships and the waterfront under columns of smoke; 7:45 to 8:50 Avengers above the clouds. Some shots are shaky.

body:
More than 350 carrier planes went after one Japanese cruiser as she got under way in Manila Bay.

13 November 1944. Admiral William Halsey's Task Force 38 struck Japanese shipping in and around Manila Bay. The planes came from Hornet, Essex, Ticonderoga, Enterprise, and four light carriers.

Their main target, the light cruiser Kiso, had orders to leave for Brunei that evening carrying Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima and his staff. Between about 8:00 and 9:23 a.m., three bombs hit her. She lost power and settled into the shallow water west of Cavite.

At Cavite, the destroyers Akishimo and Akebono were moored side by side when bombs set both ablaze. A huge explosion aboard Akishimo the next day wrecked them both. Other destroyers and transports went down too, among them Okinami, whose wreck is shown here in February 1945.

Japan salvaged Kiso's wreck in 1955 and broke her up for scrap.
